message.content:
We are going to recreate the Intellijel Metropolix as a Max4Live midi device. The Metropolix is laid out in eight stages rather than steps, delivering pitch control, four gate modes, and eight pulse counts per stage. This enables sequences up to 64 steps long. It provides two output tracks (TRK1 and TRK2) that are variants of a single master pitch/gate sequencer, programmed via pitch sliders, pulse count switches, and gate type switches. These additional tracks will have to be implemented using parameter mapping as a Max4Live device,

Regarding parameter mapping one thing of PARAMOUNT importance is solving the problem of Undo history pollution. To resolve this, All modulation output from the sequencer that targets Live parameters must use live.remote~ exclusively. Never use live.object with set for parameter values that change at sequencer rate. live.object is only permitted for one-time configuration calls (e.g. resolving a path, reading a property). The sequencer's output stage must route through live.remote~ to avoid flooding undo history. If you are unclear on how this is done, research it.

Additionally, each track has its own playback order, sequence length, clock division, swing amount, slide time, and gate lengths. Additional track menu settings include pitch slider inversion, sequence note range, and track transposition. Both tracks also have multiple lanes of per-stage playback parameters, including gate override, pitch override, ratchet count, probability of playback, accumulating transposition, and a dedicated CV/CC lane. For our purposes, the dedicated CV/CC lane can just be another parameter mapping.

Metropolix contains eight internal modulation lanes, each offering eight stages of stored values that can be routed to the assignable A or B outputs, or a plethora of internal parameters. Each mod lane has its own independent playback order, length, and clock division, enabling sophisticated self-modulation. Metropolix has dedicated pitch/gate outputs for both Track 1 and Track 2, plus two totally user-assignable outputs (A and B) with internal mod routing. Three AUX inputs allow external modulation of assignable sequencer parameters, we should at least expose these as visible UI parameters such that other devices can modulate these parameters. 

There's also some live performance features ("Loopy" mode) which allow the user to play back short sub sequences or play the stage buttons direclty like a keyboard-- we can leave this out of our implementation. There is a built in quantizer which offers 100 different scales arranged by class and you can design and modulate between custom scales and root notes. There are also ctrl knobs, aux inputs, mod lanes to modulate the bpm and clock outputs-- these we definitely DO want in our implementation.

There are also presets and storage (up to 64 preset configurations) fto recall settings. In our implementation, we can most likely use the pattr object.

Since this is an extremely dense project, I want you to spin up a team of 8 agents to read through metropolix_menu.pdf, and create a step by step implementation plan of this sequencer. It is best to chunk the feature development into discrete stages rather than attempting to tackle the entire project at once. Feature implementation order should be considered. I want all 8 agents to corroborate their research together, and decide on a final step by step implementation plan, and write it to a single markdown file. Again, they should use discretion in their development of an implementation plan-- certain features simply don't make sense as a max4live midi device, such as the run button. But otherwise, we want to recreate it as faithfully as possible, including the more advanced features such as ACCUM, and RATCHETING, etc.

The 8 agents should be thorough in their implementation plan-- use discretion for things like multiple outputs-- remember that these should probably be parameter mappings, since a single max4live midi device can only output pitch to the track that it is loaded onto, so the additional tracks are best implemented as parameter mappings. Things like this the agents should think deeply about.

Once you understand what I've told you, create the team of 8 Agents and have them begin work on readiung the pdf and writing the implementation plan markdown file.

   525→This device complies with Part 15 of the FCC Rules. Operation is subject to
   526→the following two conditions: (1) this device may not cause harmful
   527→interference, and (2) this device must accept any interference received,
   528→including interference that may cause undesired operation.
   529→Changes or modifications not expressly approved by Intellijel Designs, Inc.
   530→could void the user’s authority to operate the equipment.
   531→Any digital equipment has been tested and found to comply with the limits for a
   532→Class A digital device, pursuant to part 15 of the FCC Rules. These limits are
   533→designed to provide reasonable protection against harmful interference when
   534→the equipment is operated in a commercial environment. This equipment
   535→generates, uses, and can radiate radio frequency energy and, if not installed
   536→and used in accordance with the instruction manual, may cause harmful
   537→interference to radio communications.
   538→
   539→This device meets the requirements of the following standards and directives:
   540→EMC: 2014/30/EU
   541→EN55032:2015 ; EN55103-2:2009 (EN55024) ; EN61000-3-2 ; EN61000-3-3
   542→Low Voltage: 2014/35/EU
   543→EN 60065:2002+A1:2006+A11:2008+A2:2010+A12:2011
   544→RoHS2: 2011/65/EU
   545→WEEE: 2012/19/EU
   546→
   547→Metropolix Manual
   548→
   549→6
   550→
   551→ INSTALLATION
   552→Intellijel Eurorack modules are designed to be used with a Eurorack-compatible case and power
   553→supply. We recommend you use Intellijel cases and power supplies.
   554→Before installing a new module in your case, you must ensure your power supply has a free power
   555→header and sufficient available capacity to power the module:
   556→●
   557→
   558→Sum up the specified +12V current draw for all modules, including the new one. Do the same for
   559→the -12 V and +5V current draw. The current draw will be specified in the manufacturer's
   560→technical specifications for each module.
   561→
   562→●
   563→
   564→Compare each of the sums to specifications for your case’s power supply.
   565→
   566→●
   567→
   568→Only proceed with installation if none of the values exceeds the power supply’s specifications.
   569→Otherwise you must remove modules to free up capacity or upgrade your power supply.
   570→
   571→You will also need to ensure your case has enough free space (hp) to fit the new module. To
   572→prevent screws or other debris from falling into the case and shorting any electrical contacts, do not
   573→leave gaps between adjacent modules, and cover all unused areas with blank panels. Similarly, do
   574→not use open frames or any other enclosure that exposes the backside of any module or the power
   575→distribution board.
   576→You can use a tool like ModularGrid to assist in your planning. Failure to adequately power your
   577→modules may result in damage to your modules or power supply. If you are unsure, please contact
   578→us before proceeding.
   579→
   580→Metropolix Manual
   581→
   582→7
   583→
   584→ Installing Your Module
   585→When installing or removing a module from your case always turn off the power to the case and
   586→disconnect the power cable. Failure to do so may result in serious injury or equipment damage.
   587→Ensure the 10-pin connector on the power cable is
   588→connected correctly to the module before
   589→proceeding. The red stripe on the cable must line up
   590→with the -12V pins on the module’s power connector.
   591→Different modules use different ways to indicate the
   592→-12V pins. Some may be labelled with “-12V;” a white
   593→stripe next to the -12V pins; the words “red stripe;” or
   594→some combination of these. Additionally, some
   595→modules may have shrouded headers, thus
   596→preventing backward connections.
   597→Most modules will come with the cable already
   598→connected but it is good to double check the
   599→orientation. Be aware that some modules may have
   600→headers that serve other purposes so ensure the
   601→power cable is connected to the right one.
   602→The other end of the cable, with a 16-pin connector,
   603→connects to the power bus board of your Eurorack
   604→case. Ensure the red stripe on the cable lines up with
   605→the -12V pins on the bus board. On Intellijel power
   606→supplies the pins are labelled with the label “-12V”
   607→and a thick white stripe. Sometimes the connectors
   608→are shrouded, ensuring the cable can only be
   609→oriented in one direction.
   610→If you are using another manufacturer’s power
   611→supply, check their documentation for instructions.
   612→
   613→Metropolix Manual
   614→
   615→8
   616→
   617→ Once connected, the cabling between the module and power supply should resemble the picture
   618→below:
   619→Before reconnecting power and
   620→turning on your modular system,
   621→double check that the ribbon cable is
   622→fully seated on both ends and that all
   623→the pins are correctly aligned. If the
   624→pins are misaligned in any direction or
   625→the ribbon is backwards you can
   626→cause damage to your module, power
   627→supply, or other modules.
   628→After you have confirmed all the
   629→connections, you can reconnect the
   630→power cable and turn on your modular
   631→system. You should immediately
   632→check that all your modules have powered on and are functioning correctly. If you notice any
   633→anomalies, turn your system off right away and check your cabling again for mistakes.

   636→You can connect an Intellijel Gx (or Qx) gate expander module to Metropolix to provide eight
   637→additional gate and trigger outputs, which you configure via the MX button on the Metropolix panel.
   638→1. Turn off power to your eurorack system.
   639→2. Using the power power cable included with your expander module (Gx or Qx), connect one end
   640→to the module’s 10-pin power connector and the other to the 16-pin power socket on your
   641→eurorack system’s powered bus board — paying attention to polarity (aligning the red stripe as
   642→described previously).
   643→3. Using the I2C cable included with your expander module, connect one end to the module’s 6-pin
   644→I2C connector and the other end to the I2C port on your Metropolix module. Both ports are
   645→shrouded to ensure they can be connected in only one direction.
   646→4. Power up your eurorack system.
   647→IMPORTANT !!! : Always power down the modules before connecting or disconnecting an
   648→I2C cable.
   649→
   650→Metropolix Manual
   651→
   652→9
   653→
   654→ METROPOLIX OVERVIEW
   655→The Intellijel Metropolix is a unique and powerful Eurorack format musical sequencer, which evolves
   656→and expands upon the real-time, hands-on, dynamic sequencing methodology first introduced in the
   657→Intellijel Metropolis (which was, itself, inspired by the original Ryk M-185 — a Roland System 100m
   658→format sequencer).
   659→On first blush, it appears to be a simple 8-stage sequencer — but there is far more functionality than
   660→first meets the eye:
   661→●
   662→
   663→There are two tracks (TRK 1 and TRK 2) that are variants of the single main pitch/gate
   664→sequencer, which is programmed via the PITCH sliders, PULSE COUNT and GATE TYPE
   665→switches. Each track interprets the sequence in a variety of ways — creating complementary
   666→sequence variations that enable you to generate counterpoint, polyrhythms, and all manner of
   667→sonic movement (both subtle and extreme).
   668→Each of these tracks has its own playback ORDER, sequence LENgth, clock DIVision, SWING
   669→amount, SLIDE time, and track GATE lengths. Other track-based sequence variables are
   670→accessible from the TRACK MENU, and include Pitch Slider inversion; sequence note range;
   671→track transposition; and more. In addition, Tracks 1 & 2 both have multiple lanes of per-stage
   672→playback parameters, including: GATE override; PITCH override; RATCHet count; PROBability
   673→of playback; ACCUMulating transposition, and a dedicated CV lane. Each stage also has a
   674→SKIP feature, and a pitch SLIDE option.
   675→
   676→●
   677→
   678→8 separate and individual MODulation lanes are accessed via the MOD button. Each MOD lane
   679→has 8-stages of modulation values and its own playback ORDER, LENgth, and clock DIVision;
   680→and each lane is routable to one of Metropolix’ two assignable outputs or to dozens of internal
   681→destinations, allowing for some sophisticated and powerful self-modulation.
   682→
   683→●
   684→
   685→A trio of AUX inputs allows for external modulation of user-assignable sequencer parameters for
   686→even greater variation, while two assignable CTRL knobs give you direct access to the
   687→parameters you want to adjust most frequently during a performance. With dedicated Pitch/Gate
   688→outputs for both Track 1 and Track 2; two totally user-assignable outputs (A and B); and internal
   689→MOD routing, Metropolix features a wealth of patching opportunities.
   690→
   691→●
   692→
   693→Metropolix also features a Loopy mode, allowing you to instantly play back short
   694→sub-sequences, or even “play” the stage buttons directly (like a ‘keyboard’).
   695→
   696→Metropolix Manual

   698→10
   699→
   700→ ●
   701→
   702→Metropolix stores up to 64 preset configurations (in 8 banks of 8 presets), and all live settings
   703→are stored in EPROM, ensuring that your Metropolix will always power up exactly as you left it
   704→— even if you haven’t saved them to a preset. By default presets can change all the structural
   705→(menu-based) elements of your sequencer without overwriting the front panel controls, but full
   706→recall is also available.
   707→
   708→●
   709→
   710→The operation of the Metropolix is optimized for live performance and jamming, with quick
   711→access to all the most important performance parameters, and the ability to greatly affect your
   712→sequences with a single slider or switch.
   713→

   715→●
   716→
   717→Bold text = BUTTON names and JACK names.
   718→
   719→●
   720→
   721→Monospace text = Screen Parameter NAMES
   722→
   723→●
   724→
   725→‘Quoted’ text = Parameter ‘values’
   726→
   727→●
   728→
   729→When told to long-press a button, it means to press the button down and hold it for
   730→approximately 1 second. Some buttons have secondary functions, and long-pressing a button is
   731→the way to access these secondary functions.
   732→
   733→●
   734→
   735→When told to press-hold or press-and-hold a button, it means to press a button and continue to
   736→hold it down while pressing a second button.

   740→11
   741→
   742→ FRONT PANEL OVERVIEW
   743→The Front Panel consists of numerous input and output jacks, plus a plethora of buttons, switches,
   744→knobs, and other such controllers.
   745→
   746→Each of these is described briefly below, though more detailed descriptions are contained later in
   747→the manual.

   750→
   751→12
   752→
   753→ OUTPUTS
   754→[A]
   755→
   756→A OUT - The first of two user assignable signals is sent out this jack. To assign a signal to this
   757→jack, press the ALT button to enter ALT mode, then press the A (Stage 3) button, as
   758→described in OUT A & B, later in this manual.
   759→The color of the output LED changes depending on the type of signal it carries
   760→(blue = pitch/root data; yellow = gate/trigger; green (+) / red (-) = continuous voltage).
   761→
   762→[B]
   763→
   764→B OUT - The second of two user assignable signals is sent out this jack. To assign a signal to
   765→this jack, press the ALT button to enter ALT mode, then press the B (Stage 4) button, as
   766→described in OUT A & B, later in this manual. As with the A output, the color of its
   767→corresponding LED indicates the type of signal assigned to it.
   768→
   769→[C]
   770→
   771→CLOCK OUT - Outputs a clock from Metropolix. A clock signal is output only when the
   772→sequencer is running. The output clock can run at any division of the input (whether internally
   773→or externally clocked), as set by the Clk Div parameter accessed via the ALT + CLK
   774→(Stage 5) button, as discussed in CLK, later in this manual.
   775→
   776→[D]
   777→
   778→TRACK 1 PITCH OUT - By default, the 1 V/Oct pitch generated by Track 1 is sent out this
   779→jack. However, it’s possible to swap Track assignments, such that Track 2’s pitch is sent to this
   780→jack. This feature (called Trk Out Swap) can be assigned to a CTRL knob or an AUX input or
   781→MOD Lane.
   782→
   783→[E]
   784→
   785→TRACK 1 GATE OUT - By default, Track 1’s gate signal (off = 0V; on = +5V) is sent out this
   786→jack. However, like with the PITCH out, you can swap it to carry Track 2’s gate output instead.
   787→The corresponding LED lights whenever the gate output is high (on).
   788→
   789→[F]
   790→
   791→TRACK 2 PITCH OUT - By default, the 1 V/Oct pitch generated by Track 2 is sent out this
   792→jack. However, it’s possible to swap Track assignments, such that Track 1’s pitch is sent to this
   793→jack. This feature (called Trk Out Swap) can be assigned to a CTRL knob or an AUX input or
   794→MOD Lane.
   795→
   796→[G]
   797→
   798→TRACK 2 GATE OUT - By default, Track 2’s gate signal (off = 0V; on = +5V) is sent out this
   799→jack. However, like with the PITCH output, you can swap it to carry Track 1’s gate output
   800→instead. The corresponding LED lights whenever the gate output is high (on).
   801→
   802→Metropolix Manual
   803→
   804→13
   805→
   806→ INPUTS
   807→[H]
   808→
   809→CLOCK IN - Patch an external clock source here. This input is used to synchronize Metropolix
   810→playback to an external signal source, and requires that Metropolex be clocked externally
   811→(which is enabled by pressing the SETUP button, and setting Clock to ‘External’).
   812→NOTE: The Clock IN LED blinks in time with the clock division being applied to this incoming
   813→external clock (as set with the Ext Clock Div parameter on the BPM screen, when
   814→Clock = ’External’. The LED does not blink if the internal clock is used.
   815→
   816→[I]
   817→
   818→RESET IN - By default, a trigger signal patched into this jack will reset the current sequence to
   819→its beginning stage.
   820→You can program individual tracks to ignore the RESET trigger by going to the TRACK MENU,
   821→and setting the Global Reset option to ‘Off.’
   822→Using the SETUP MENU, you can reconfigure the jack to act as a RUN input (instead of a
   823→RESET input). In this configuration, the sequence plays while the input gate signal is high, and
   824→it doesn’t play when the gate signal is low.
   825→NOTE: The LED above the RESET jack flashes red each time the sequence resets.
   826→
   827→[X]
   828→
   829→X IN - One of three AUX inputs for controlling Metropolix. Patch a control voltage source (-5V
   830→to +5V) into this jack to modulate whichever sequencer parameter is assigned to that jack.
   831→See AUX Input Settings to learn how to assign parameters to the X IN jack, and what those
   832→various parameters accomplish.
   833→
   834→[Y]
   835→
   836→Y IN - A second AUX input for controlling Metropolix. It is functionally identical to the X IN.
   837→
   838→[Z]
   839→
   840→Z IN - A third AUX input for controlling Metropolix. It, too, is functionally identical to X IN.
   841→
   842→Metropolix Manual
   843→
   844→14
   845→
   846→ SECTIONS
   847→In order to understand all the various control features, let’s first look at how they’re grouped:
   848→[1]
   849→
   850→PITCH sliders - These eight sliders control the pitch played by the associated stage. See
   851→PITCH SLIDERS for more information.
   852→
   853→[2]
   854→
   855→PULSE COUNT switches - Each of these switches sets the pulse count (from 1 to 8 pulses)
   856→for the corresponding stage. This determines how long the stage plays in relation to all the
   857→other stages. See PULSE COUNT for more information.
   858→
   859→[3]
   860→
   861→GATE TYPE switches - Each switch sets the gate type for its respective stage, either HOLD,
   862→MULTIPLE, SINGLE, or REST as discussed in GATE TYPES, later in this manual.
   863→
   864→[4]
   865→
   866→SCREEN & TRACK BUTTONS - This section, discussed in SCREEN & TRACK BUTTONS,
   867→contains a SCREEN and PUSH-ENCODER for setting and viewing Metropolix functions; three
   868→TRACK buttons for selecting which track you wish to edit (TRK 1, TRK 2 or MOD Lanes); and
   869→an EXIT button, which exits any open menus and/or returns the screen to Metropolix’ top-level
   870→HOME Screen.
   871→
   872→[5]
   873→
   874→TRANSPORT Buttons - These buttons control Metropolix’s transport, enabling you to start
   875→and stop playback, reset the sequencer to its ‘starting’ position, and enter Loopy mode. See
   876→TRANSPORT BUTTONS for a detailed description.
   877→
   878→[6]
   879→
   880→GLOBAL SETTINGS - These buttons control various functions that apply to Metropolix as a
   881→whole — operating across all tracks. See GLOBAL SETTINGS for a detailed description of all
   882→the GLOBAL SETTINGS buttons.
   883→
   884→[7]
   885→
   886→TRACK SETTINGS - These buttons modify the track that’s currently selected for editing.
   887→Tracks are selected by pressing (and lighting) the corresponding TRACK button in the
   888→SCREEN & TRACK BUTTONS section. See TRACK SETTINGS for a detailed description of
   889→all the TRACK SETTINGS buttons.
   890→
   891→[8]
   892→
   893→STAGE Buttons - These buttons modify different settings on a stage-by-stage basis within
   894→individual tracks. See STAGE BUTTONS for a detailed description of every STAGE function.
   895→
   896→[9]
   897→
   898→ALT Buttons - Each Stage button has an alternate function, indicated by the text above the
   899→button, which is accessed by pressing the ALT button prior to pressing the Stage button. See
   900→ALT BUTTONS for a detailed description of all the ALT functions.
   901→
   902→[10] CTRL (Control) Knobs - Assign functions to each of these knobs for real-time changes
   903→during a performance. See Control Knobs for a detailed description of these knobs.
   904→[11] AUX IN Settings - Metropolix offers three user-assignable AUX inputs (X, Y and Z) for
   905→controlling the sequencer externally. Press an input’s corresponding button to assign an AUX
   906→destination on one or more tracks, and use the built-in attenuverter to dial in the desired
   907→amount of control. For more information, see AUX Input Settings.
   908→
   909→Metropolix Manual
   910→
   911→15
   912→
   913→ PITCH SLIDERS
   914→(SECTION 1)
   915→
   916→These sliders determine the default pitch value of each corresponding stage. Metropolix uses the
   917→position of these sliders as a starting point for determining the actual pitch output by each stage on
   918→each track.
   919→On a GLOBAL level:
   920→●
   921→
   922→Via the SCALE button, you can assign a scale type and root note to any quantized slider.
   923→
   924→●
   925→
   926→Via the SETUP button, you can define which note represents the bottom of the slider (either a
   927→“C” or the current scale’s root note).
   928→
   929→On a per-TRACK level (accessed via the TRACK MENU), you can assign:
   930→●
   931→
   932→The pitch range of the slider (from 1 octave bottom-to-top, to 4 octaves bottom-to-top)
   933→
   934→●
   935→
   936→Whether the slider’s lowest pitch is at the bottom (normal) or at the top (inverted).
   937→
   938→●
   939→
   940→An overall output transposition above or below the default pitch value (±60 semitones).
   941→
   942→Metropolix Manual
   943→
   944→16
   945→
   946→ On a per-STAGE, per-TRACK level:
   947→●
   948→
   949→Via the PITCH button, you can assign a note value that deviates from the slider’s current
   950→position for each stage on each track.
   951→
   952→●
   953→
   954→Via the ACCUM button, you can assign whether a stage’s pitch transposes cumulatively (either
   955→with each pass through the stage; each pulse within a stage; or each ratchet).
   956→
   957→The way in which a slider’s position can be interpreted, inverted, transposed and overridden by the
   958→various tracks and stages allows Metropolix to create harmonic intervals and counterpoint that
   959→change and evolve with a single move of a slider.
   960→Each pitch slider has an LED that lights to indicate which stage is playing — glowing brightest when
   961→the stage’s gate is high and dimmer with the stage’s gate is low.
   962→When you move a pitch slider, the value will be shown briefly on the screen, enabling you to set
   963→pitch values quickly and precisely.
   964→
   965→The keyboard ‘greys out’ (hashes) any notes not contained within the root/scale assignment you
   966→make with the SCALE button. That is, in-scale white keys are white; in-scale black keys are black;
   967→out-of scale keys (black or white) are ‘grey.’ The note you select with the pitch slider is indicated by
   968→a dot (and named beneath the keyboard, on the right). The Stage Number is shown beneath the
   969→keyboard on the left. Note that setting a Transpose value in the Track Menu enables you to assign
   970→notes that are out of scale.
   971→NOTE: Metropolix offers the option of loading stored pitch values with a Preset in its SETUP menu.
   972→If you choose to load this data, then the pitch you hear may not match the sliders. Similarly if a
   973→Stage is programmed to override the PITCH, or it’s being modulated by an AUX input, or the
   974→ACCUM function is operating, it too will override the slider. You can always see exactly which pitch
   975→is playing by pressing the EXIT button (to view the HOME screens), then rotating the encoder to
   976→display HOME Screen 2 : Note Overview.
   977→
   978→Metropolix Manual
   979→
   980→17
   981→
   982→ PULSE COUNT
   983→(SECTION 2)
   984→
   985→These switches set the number of clock pulses at which the sequencer stays on a particular stage.
   986→In general, the sequence will not advance to the next stage until the chosen number of clock pulses
   987→has passed. Each stage’s pulse count can be set from 1 pulse to 8 pulses.
   988→EXAMPLE: If the sequencer is currently on a stage with PULSE COUNT = 1 it will advance to
   989→the next stage (as determined by the ORDER screen) upon receipt of the next clock pulse. If the
   990→stage’s PULSE COUNT = 3, it will stay on the stage for 3 clock pulses before advancing.
   991→In general, the type (and number) of gates generated while on a stage is determined by the
   992→GATE TYPE switches (described below).
   993→NOTE: Metropolix offers the option of loading switch positions with a Preset in its SETUP menu. If
   994→you choose to load this data, then the pulse count you hear may not match the switches. You can
   995→always see the currently used switch setting by pressing the EXIT button (to view the HOME
   996→screens), then rotating the encoder to display HOME Screen 3 : Panel Values & Preset Overrides.
   997→For more general information about Pulses, see Understanding Pulse Hierarchy, later in this
   998→manual.

 COMPLIANCE
This device complies with Part 15 of the FCC Rules. Operation is subject to

Metropolix Manual

6

 INSTALLATION
Intellijel Eurorack modules are designed to be used with a Eurorack-compatible case and power
supply. We recommend you use Intellijel cases and power supplies.
Before installing a new module in your case, you must ensure your power supply has a free power
header and sufficient available capacity to power the module:
●

Sum up the specified +12V current draw for all modules, including the new one. Do the same for
the -12 V and +5V current draw. The current draw will be specified in the manufacturer's
technical specifications for each module.

●

Compare each of the sums to specifications for your case’s power supply.

●

Only proceed with installation if none of the values exceeds the power supply’s specifications.
Otherwise you must remove modules to free up capacity or upgrade your power supply.

You will also need to ensure your case has enough free space (hp) to fit the new module. To
prevent screws or other debris from falling into the case and shorting any electrical contacts, do not
leave gaps between adjacent modules, and cover all unused areas with blank panels. Similarly, do
not use open frames or any other enclosure that exposes the backside of any module or the power
distribution board.
You can use a tool like ModularGrid to assist in your planning. Failure to adequately power your
modules may result in damage to your modules or power supply. If you are unsure, please contact
us before proceeding.

Metropolix Manual

7

 Installing Your Module
When installing or removing a module from your case always turn off the power to the case and
disconnect the power cable. Failure to do so may result in serious injury or equipment damage.
Ensure the 10-pin connector on the power cable is
connected correctly to the module before
proceeding. The red stripe on the cable must line up
with the -12V pins on the module’s power connector.
Different modules use different ways to indicate the
-12V pins. Some may be labelled with “-12V;” a white
stripe next to the -12V pins; the words “red stripe;” or
some combination of these. Additionally, some
modules may have shrouded headers, thus
preventing backward connections.
Most modules will come with the cable already
connected but it is good to double check the
orientation. Be aware that some modules may have
headers that serve other purposes so ensure the
power cable is connected to the right one.
The other end of the cable, with a 16-pin connector,
connects to the power bus board of your Eurorack
case. Ensure the red stripe on the cable lines up with
the -12V pins on the bus board. On Intellijel power
supplies the pins are labelled with the label “-12V”
and a thick white stripe. Sometimes the connectors
are shrouded, ensuring the cable can only be
oriented in one direction.
If you are using another manufacturer’s power
supply, check their documentation for instructions.

Metropolix Manual

8

 Once connected, the cabling between the module and power supply should resemble the picture
below:
Before reconnecting power and
turning on your modular system,
double check that the ribbon cable is
fully seated on both ends and that all
the pins are correctly aligned. If the
pins are misaligned in any direction or
the ribbon is backwards you can
cause damage to your module, power
supply, or other modules.
After you have confirmed all the
connections, you can reconnect the
power cable and turn on your modular
system. You should immediately
check that all your modules have powered on and are functioning correctly. If you notice any
anomalies, turn your system off right away and check your cabling again for mistakes.

Connecting an Optional Expander Module
You can connect an Intellijel Gx (or Qx) gate expander module to Metropolix to provide eight
additional gate and trigger outputs, which you configure via the MX button on the Metropolix panel.
1. Turn off power to your eurorack system.
2. Using the power power cable included with your expander module (Gx or Qx), connect one end
to the module’s 10-pin power connector and the other to the 16-pin power socket on your
eurorack system’s powered bus board — paying attention to polarity (aligning the red stripe as
described previously).
3. Using the I2C cable included with your expander module, connect one end to the module’s 6-pin
I2C connector and the other end to the I2C port on your Metropolix module. Both ports are
shrouded to ensure they can be connected in only one direction.
4. Power up your eurorack system.
IMPORTANT !!! : Always power down the modules before connecting or disconnecting an
I2C cable.

●

●

●

11

 FRONT PANEL OVERVIEW
The Front Panel consists of numerous input and output jacks, plus a plethora of buttons, switches,
knobs, and other such controllers.

Each of these is described briefly below, though more detailed descriptions are contained later in
the manual.

Metropolix Manual

12

 OUTPUTS
[A]

A OUT - The first of two user assignable signals is sent out this jack. To assign a signal to this
jack, press the ALT button to enter ALT mode, then press the A (Stage 3) button, as
described in OUT A & B, later in this manual.
The color of the output LED changes depending on the type of signal it carries
(blue = pitch/root data; yellow = gate/trigger; green (+) / red (-) = continuous voltage).

[B]

B OUT - The second of two user assignable signals is sent out this jack. To assign a signal to
this jack, press the ALT button to enter ALT mode, then press the B (Stage 4) button, as
described in OUT A & B, later in this manual. As with the A output, the color of its
corresponding LED indicates the type of signal assigned to it.

[C]

CLOCK OUT - Outputs a clock from Metropolix. A clock signal is output only when the
sequencer is running. The output clock can run at any division of the input (whether internally
or externally clocked), as set by the Clk Div parameter accessed via the ALT + CLK
(Stage 5) button, as discussed in CLK, later in this manual.

[D]

TRACK 1 PITCH OUT - By default, the 1 V/Oct pitch generated by Track 1 is sent out this
jack. However, it’s possible to swap Track assignments, such that Track 2’s pitch is sent to this
jack. This feature (called Trk Out Swap) can be assigned to a CTRL knob or an AUX input or
MOD Lane.

[E]

TRACK 1 GATE OUT - By default, Track 1’s gate signal (off = 0V; on = +5V) is sent out this
jack. However, like with the PITCH out, you can swap it to carry Track 2’s gate output instead.
The corresponding LED lights whenever the gate output is high (on).

[F]

TRACK 2 PITCH OUT - By default, the 1 V/Oct pitch generated by Track 2 is sent out this
jack. However, it’s possible to swap Track assignments, such that Track 1’s pitch is sent to this
jack. This feature (called Trk Out Swap) can be assigned to a CTRL knob or an AUX input or
MOD Lane.

[G]

TRACK 2 GATE OUT - By default, Track 2’s gate signal (off = 0V; on = +5V) is sent out this
jack. However, like with the PITCH output, you can swap it to carry Track 1’s gate output
instead. The corresponding LED lights whenever the gate output is high (on).

Metropolix Manual

13

 INPUTS
[H]

CLOCK IN - Patch an external clock source here. This input is used to synchronize Metropolix
playback to an external signal source, and requires that Metropolex be clocked externally
(which is enabled by pressing the SETUP button, and setting Clock to ‘External’).
NOTE: The Clock IN LED blinks in time with the clock division being applied to this incoming
external clock (as set with the Ext Clock Div parameter on the BPM screen, when
Clock = ’External’. The LED does not blink if the internal clock is used.

[I]

RESET IN - By default, a trigger signal patched into this jack will reset the current sequence to
its beginning stage.
You can program individual tracks to ignore the RESET trigger by going to the TRACK MENU,
and setting the Global Reset option to ‘Off.’
Using the SETUP MENU, you can reconfigure the jack to act as a RUN input (instead of a
RESET input). In this configuration, the sequence plays while the input gate signal is high, and
it doesn’t play when the gate signal is low.
NOTE: The LED above the RESET jack flashes red each time the sequence resets.

[X]

X IN - One of three AUX inputs for controlling Metropolix. Patch a control voltage source (-5V
to +5V) into this jack to modulate whichever sequencer parameter is assigned to that jack.
See AUX Input Settings to learn how to assign parameters to the X IN jack, and what those
various parameters accomplish.

[Y]

Y IN - A second AUX input for controlling Metropolix. It is functionally identical to the X IN.

[Z]

Z IN - A third AUX input for controlling Metropolix. It, too, is functionally identical to X IN.

Metropolix Manual

14

 SECTIONS
In order to understand all the various control features, let’s first look at how they’re grouped:
[1]

PITCH sliders - These eight sliders control the pitch played by the associated stage. See
PITCH SLIDERS for more information.

[2]

PULSE COUNT switches - Each of these switches sets the pulse count (from 1 to 8 pulses)
for the corresponding stage. This determines how long the stage plays in relation to all the
other stages. See PULSE COUNT for more information.

[3]

GATE TYPE switches - Each switch sets the gate type for its respective stage, either HOLD,
MULTIPLE, SINGLE, or REST as discussed in GATE TYPES, later in this manual.

[4]

SCREEN & TRACK BUTTONS - This section, discussed in SCREEN & TRACK BUTTONS,
contains a SCREEN and PUSH-ENCODER for setting and viewing Metropolix functions; three
TRACK buttons for selecting which track you wish to edit (TRK 1, TRK 2 or MOD Lanes); and
an EXIT button, which exits any open menus and/or returns the screen to Metropolix’ top-level
HOME Screen.

[5]

TRANSPORT Buttons - These buttons control Metropolix’s transport, enabling you to start
and stop playback, reset the sequencer to its ‘starting’ position, and enter Loopy mode. See
TRANSPORT BUTTONS for a detailed description.

[6]

GLOBAL SETTINGS - These buttons control various functions that apply to Metropolix as a
whole — operating across all tracks. See GLOBAL SETTINGS for a detailed description of all
the GLOBAL SETTINGS buttons.

[7]

TRACK SETTINGS - These buttons modify the track that’s currently selected for editing.
Tracks are selected by pressing (and lighting) the corresponding TRACK button in the
SCREEN & TRACK BUTTONS section. See TRACK SETTINGS for a detailed description of
all the TRACK SETTINGS buttons.

[8]

STAGE Buttons - These buttons modify different settings on a stage-by-stage basis within
individual tracks. See STAGE BUTTONS for a detailed description of every STAGE function.

[9]

ALT Buttons - Each Stage button has an alternate function, indicated by the text above the
button, which is accessed by pressing the ALT button prior to pressing the Stage button. See
ALT BUTTONS for a detailed description of all the ALT functions.

[10] CTRL (Control) Knobs - Assign functions to each of these knobs for real-time changes
during a performance. See Control Knobs for a detailed description of these knobs.
[11] AUX IN Settings - Metropolix offers three user-assignable AUX inputs (X, Y and Z) for
controlling the sequencer externally. Press an input’s corresponding button to assign an AUX
destination on one or more tracks, and use the built-in attenuverter to dial in the desired
amount of control. For more information, see AUX Input Settings.

Metropolix Manual

15

 PITCH SLIDERS
(SECTION 1)

These sliders determine the default pitch value of each corresponding stage. Metropolix uses the
position of these sliders as a starting point for determining the actual pitch output by each stage on
each track.
On a GLOBAL level:
●

Via the SCALE button, you can assign a scale type and root note to any quantized slider.

●

Via the SETUP button, you can define which note represents the bottom of the slider (either a
“C” or the current scale’s root note).

On a per-TRACK level (accessed via the TRACK MENU), you can assign:
●

The pitch range of the slider (from 1 octave bottom-to-top, to 4 octaves bottom-to-top)

●

Whether the slider’s lowest pitch is at the bottom (normal) or at the top (inverted).

●

An overall output transposition above or below the default pitch value (±60 semitones).

Metropolix Manual

16

 On a per-STAGE, per-TRACK level:
●

Via the PITCH button, you can assign a note value that deviates from the slider’s current
position for each stage on each track.

●

Via the ACCUM button, you can assign whether a stage’s pitch transposes cumulatively (either
with each pass through the stage; each pulse within a stage; or each ratchet).

The way in which a slider’s position can be interpreted, inverted, transposed and overridden by the
various tracks and stages allows Metropolix to create harmonic intervals and counterpoint that
change and evolve with a single move of a slider.
Each pitch slider has an LED that lights to indicate which stage is playing — glowing brightest when
the stage’s gate is high and dimmer with the stage’s gate is low.
When you move a pitch slider, the value will be shown briefly on the screen, enabling you to set
pitch values quickly and precisely.

The keyboard ‘greys out’ (hashes) any notes not contained within the root/scale assignment you
make with the SCALE button. That is, in-scale white keys are white; in-scale black keys are black;
out-of scale keys (black or white) are ‘grey.’ The note you select with the pitch slider is indicated by
a dot (and named beneath the keyboard, on the right). The Stage Number is shown beneath the
keyboard on the left. Note that setting a Transpose value in the Track Menu enables you to assign
notes that are out of scale.
NOTE: Metropolix offers the option of loading stored pitch values with a Preset in its SETUP menu.
If you choose to load this data, then the pitch you hear may not match the sliders. Similarly if a
Stage is programmed to override the PITCH, or it’s being modulated by an AUX input, or the
ACCUM function is operating, it too will override the slider. You can always see exactly which pitch
is playing by pressing the EXIT button (to view the HOME screens), then rotating the encoder to
display HOME Screen 2 : Note Overview.

Metropolix Manual

17

 PULSE COUNT
(SECTION 2)

These switches set the number of clock pulses at which the sequencer stays on a particular stage.
In general, the sequence will not advance to the next stage until the chosen number of clock pulses
has passed. Each stage’s pulse count can be set from 1 pulse to 8 pulses.
EXAMPLE: If the sequencer is currently on a stage with PULSE COUNT = 1 it will advance to
the next stage (as determined by the ORDER screen) upon receipt of the next clock pulse. If the
stage’s PULSE COUNT = 3, it will stay on the stage for 3 clock pulses before advancing.
In general, the type (and number) of gates generated while on a stage is determined by the
GATE TYPE switches (described below).
NOTE: Metropolix offers the option of loading switch positions with a Preset in its SETUP menu. If
you choose to load this data, then the pulse count you hear may not match the switches. You can
always see the currently used switch setting by pressing the EXIT button (to view the HOME
screens), then rotating the encoder to display HOME Screen 3 : Panel Values & Preset Overrides.
For more general information about Pulses, see Understanding Pulse Hierarchy, later in this
manual.

  1300→are accessible via the MOD button. Specifically:
  1301→●
  1302→
  1303→TRK 1 and TRK 2 are variants of the single main pitch/gate sequencer programmed via the
  1304→PITCH sliders, PULSE COUNT and GATE TYPE switches. Each track interprets the sequence
  1305→in a variety of ways — creating complementary sequence variations that enable you to generate
  1306→counterpoint, polyrhythms, and all manner of sonic movement (both subtle and extreme).
  1307→Each of these tracks has its own playback ORDER, sequence LENgth, clock DIVision, SWING
  1308→amount, SLIDE time, and track GATE lengths. Other track-based sequence variables are
  1309→accessible from the TRACK MENU, and include Pitch Slider inversion; sequence note range;
  1310→track transposition; and more. In addition, Tracks 1 & 2 both have multiple lanes of per-stage
  1311→playback parameters, including: GATE override; PITCH override; RATCHet count; PROBability
  1312→of playback; ACCUMulated transposition, and a dedicated CV lane. Each stage also has a SKIP
  1313→feature, and a pitch SLIDE option.
  1314→
  1315→●
  1316→
  1317→MOD is a collection of 8 separate and individual modulation lanes. Each MOD Lane has
  1318→8-stages of modulation values and its own playback ORDER, LENgth, and clock DIVision; and
  1319→each lane is routable to one of Metropolix’ two assignable outputs or to dozens of internal
  1320→destinations, allowing for some sophisticated and powerful self-modulation.

  1459→ Off
  1460→
  1461→When ‘off,’ gate lengths always refer to the length of a clock pulse. If a
  1462→note extends beyond a single clock pulse, the note’s gate length does
  1463→not stretch, and the extra time is filled with rests.
  1464→For example, assume a stage has a GATE LENGTH = 50%, a
  1465→GATE TYPE = SINGLE, and a PULSE COUNT = 4. The gate will open at
  1466→the beginning of the stage and stay open for half a clock pulse, before
  1467→going low for the final 3.5 clock pulses in the stage. You can see an
  1468→example of this (and other) Gate interactions in Gate Stretching Examples, later in the manual.

  1470→Ratchets
  1471→
  1472→IMPORTANT: This parameter applies only when Gate Stretching = On
  1473→(as described above). It has no effect if a track’s Gate Stretching
  1474→parameter is turned off.
  1475→The Ratchets parameter affects the way ratchets are calculated, as
  1476→described below. See RATCH, later in the manual, for more information
  1477→about ratcheting, and numerous examples regarding the use of this
  1478→parameter.
  1479→Multiply
  1480→
  1481→When you assign ‘x’ number of ratchets to a stage, this option creates ‘x’
  1482→number of ratchets in ‘y’ pulse counts, where the value of ‘y’ is
  1483→determined by the stage’s PULSE COUNT switch plus the DIV screen’s
  1484→PULSE COUNT DIV value (if the GATE TYPE = MULTI) .
  1485→This results in ratchet repeat rates that speed up or slow down
  1486→depending on how long the non-ratched gate would last. It can yield very
  1487→interesting rhythmic variations but may not sonically resemble
  1488→“traditional” ratchets.
  1489→
  1490→Pulse
  1491→
  1492→When you assign ‘x’ number of ratchets to a stage, this option ensures
  1493→that all ‘x’ ratchets will play in the amount of time occupied by a single
  1494→clock pulse. In this case, ‘x’ determines both the repeat rate of the
  1495→ratchets, and the number of total ratchets played in a gate.
  1496→This creates the ‘classic’ ratcheting effect of sequencers from the past. It
  1497→ensures that ratchets always repeat at the same rate (regardless of Gate
  1498→length), and that the requested number of ratchets are always heard.
  1499→
  1500→Gated
  1501→
  1502→When you assign ‘x’ number of ratchets to a stage, this option ensures
  1503→that the ratchets will trigger at the rate of ‘x’ ratchets per clock pulse.
  1504→However, the actual number of ratchets played will increase (or
  1505→decrease) as the non-ratcheted gate lengths stretch or contract. In this
  1506→case, ‘x’ determines the repeat rate of the ratchets, but the Gate Length
  1507→determines the number of total ratchets played.
  1508→This is a variation on the ‘classic’ ratcheting effect, in that it ensures the
  1509→ratchets always repeat at the same rate, but it allows for the number of
  1510→ratchets to expand or contract with gate length.

  1521→
  1522→When a stage is set to GATE TYPE = REST, the stage’s pitch setting is
  1523→ignored, meaning the previous stage’s pitch is held over into the rested
  1524→stage. So if you’re using an envelope with a long decay/release, you
  1525→won’t hear the pitch change as the sequence progresses to the rested
  1526→stage, and the previous stage’s pitch will die out without changing —
  1527→exactly as you would expect a ‘rest’ to work.

  1529→Update
  1530→
  1531→When a stage is set to GATE TYPE = REST, the stage’s pitch setting is
  1532→honoured. Since a rested stage does not generate a new gate, you will
  1533→only hear this effect if you’re using an envelope in which the
  1534→decay/release time is long enough to extend into the rested stage. At this
  1535→point, you would hear the pitch change as the envelope continues to
  1536→decay. This can result in some interesting ‘ghost’ notes or (if using the
  1537→SLIDE options) a “slur”, rather than a “rest.”

  1687→ TRANSPORT BUTTONS
  1688→(SECTION 5)
  1689→
  1690→RUN
  1691→This button toggles between starting and stopping the sequencer. If the sequencer is stopped, press
  1692→RUN to start it playing in sync with the next pulse (or immediately if the pulse happens at the same
  1693→time). If the sequencer is playing, press the RUN button to stop (or pause) it immediately.
  1694→In the SETUP MENU, you can assign the RUN button to function as either a “Run/Stop” button or a
  1695→“Run/Pause” button. When configured as a “Run/Stop” button, pressing RUN while the sequencer
  1696→plays will stop the sequence and trigger a reset. When configured as a “Run/Pause” button,
  1697→pressing RUN while the sequencer plays will pause the sequence, but not reset it — meaning a
  1698→subsequent press of the RUN button will start the sequence from its current position, and not from
  1699→the beginning.
  1700→When the sequencer is stopped, the gate outputs return to 0V.
  1701→The RUN button (and the corresponding RESET jack, if configured as a RUN jack in the
  1702→SETUP MENU) will simultaneously start/stop playback of all three Metropolix tracks (TRK 1, TRK 2
  1703→and MOD). You can, however, mute and unmute individual tracks (and even individual MOD Lanes),
  1704→by holding the LOOPY button while pressing the TRACK button or MOD Lane button that you want
  1705→muted. For more information, see Muting Tracks and MOD Lanes.
  1706→NOTE : In order to run, Metropolix needs a clock, either internally generated or externally supplied.
  1707→See the CLK section, later in this manual, to learn about the different ways to clock Metropolix.
  1708→
  1709→RESET
  1710→This button manually resets the sequencer. The reset is synchronized to the first clock pulse after
  1711→you press the RESET button. When the sequencer is reset, the stage position returns to its original
  1712→starting stage and the Cumulative Transpose counters are reset.
  1713→The RESET button (and the corresponding RESET jack, if configured as a RESET jack in the
  1714→SETUP MENU) simultaneously resets all Metropolix tracks and MOD Lanes. That is, it’s a global
  1715→reset. It will also set the Track 1 and Track 2 GATE outputs to 0v.
  1716→NOTE: To reset only a single Track (or all MOD Lanes), hold-down the desired button (TRK 1,
  1717→TRK 2 or MOD) while pressing the RESET button.
  1718→

  1722→
  1723→ LOOPY (∞)
  1724→Press the ∞ (LOOPY) button to activate Metropolix’s Loopy mode.
  1725→Loopy enables you to interject a short, linear sub-loop into the current sequencer pattern, which will
  1726→play either forward or backward, depending on the ORDER Screen’s Direction parameter.
  1727→You can set the beginning stage of this sub-loop by pressing and holding down a single Stage
  1728→button, and the sub-loop will play for however many pulses you set using the LOOP PULSES
  1729→parameter. If LOOP PULSES = ’Auto,’ then Loopy repeats the single stage. This technique is called
  1730→“1-Finger Loopy.”
  1731→You can hold down a second Stage button to help further define the Loopy length. Specifically,
  1732→Loopy will continue to honour the LOOP PULSES count, wrapping back around to the starting stage
  1733→if the number of LOOP PULSES exceeds the total PULSE COUNT contained in the stages. If
  1734→LOOP PULSES = ’Auto,’ then Loopy dynamically alters the loop length based on the PULSE
  1735→COUNTS of all looped stages, ensuring each Stage plays its full pulse count. This technique is
  1736→called “2-finger Loopy.”
  1737→Loopy ignores a stage’s Skip state, meaning all looped stages play, regardless of their Skip status,
  1738→and Loopy playback can be either latched or momentary.
  1739→When the track is not running, the Stage buttons all glow blue to indicate the Stage Player
  1740→functionality is active. Here, you can press any stage button to transmit that stage’s corresponding
  1741→pitch, gate and CV value. This lets you quickly set up custom ‘keyboards,’ enabling you to perform
  1742→with Stage buttons, exactly as you would perform with a keyboard.
  1743→NOTE: If you press and hold down on the LOOPY button, the three TRACK buttons and eight
  1744→STAGE/LANE buttons light yellow. Pressing a TRACK or LANE button while holding down the
  1745→LOOPY button will mute (blinking red) or unmute (yellow) the respective Track/Lane. This is
  1746→defined further in Muting Tracks and MOD Lanes.
  1747→The following sections describe Loopy Mode, the Loopy button, and the various Loopy techniques.
  1748→
  1749→Metropolix Manual
  1750→
  1751→34
  1752→
  1753→ Enter and Conﬁgure Loopy Mode
  1754→1. Press the LOOPY (∞) button to turn on Loopy mode.
  1755→If the sequencer is running, then the eight stage buttons light up in a
  1756→“Loopywave” of pink and blue. If the sequencer is stopped, the buttons
  1757→glow solid blue and can be used as a sort of ‘keyboard’ (described in the
  1758→Stage Player section, below).
  1759→The LOOPY SETTINGS screen appears with two parameters:
  1760→LOOP PULSES :
  1761→
  1762→Displays the number of pulses that will be repeatedly looped. This setting
  1763→has no effect on Loopy’s Stage Player functionality.
  1764→‘Auto’ : Primarily used by the 2-finger method, ‘Auto’ dynamically and
  1765→automatically varies the number of Loopy pulses to always play all
  1766→possible pulses between the left and right Loopy points. As you
  1767→change the Loopy end points, the pulse count changes based on
  1768→the total number of pulses contained between those two
  1769→endpoints.
  1770→1 - 64 : You can select from 1 to 64 pulses and Loopy will always play that
  1771→many pulses in a loop.
  1772→
  1773→LOOP TARGET : Indicates whether Loopy impacts only to the current track (‘Current’) or
  1774→both TRK 1 and TRK 2 (‘1+2’).
  1775→NOTE: Loopy works only with TRK 1 and TRK 2, and not on the
  1776→MOD Lanes. If the MOD button is lit when you press the LOOPY button,
  1777→Metropolix automatically switches to TRK 1, making it the ‘Current’ track.
  1778→2. Turn the encoder to set the desired number of LOOP PULSES (in number of pulses, or ‘Auto’).
  1779→3. Press the encoder to toggle whether Loopy applies only to the ‘Current’ note track (as indicated
  1780→by the lit TRK <n> button), or if it applies to both note tracks (in which case the LOOP TARGET
  1781→value reads “1+2’).
  1782→4. Use Loopy with 1-finger, 2-fingers, or as a Stage Player as discussed in their respective
  1783→sections, below.
  1784→5. Exit Loopy by pressing the EXIT button, or any of the Global Settings buttons or Track Settings
  1785→buttons).
  1786→The following sections will describe three ways to perform using Loopy (1-Finger, 2-Finger, and
  1787→Stage Player).
  1788→
  1789→Metropolix Manual
  1790→
  1791→35
  1792→
  1793→ 1-Finger Loopy
  1794→The loop begins at the Stage button being held, and lasts for the number of pulses set in the
  1795→LOOPY Screen’s LOOP PULSES field.
  1796→Specifically:
  1797→1. Enter and configure Loopy as described in Enter and Configure Loopy Mode.
  1798→2. If the sequencer is currently stopped, press the RUN button (or use one of the remote RUN
  1799→options) to start track playback.
  1800→The eight stage buttons light up in a “Loopywave” of pink and blue, and the Action Display on
  1801→the screen reads “Loop Stage(s)”.
  1802→3. Press and hold one of the eight Stage buttons.
  1803→Beginning with the next clock pulse, playback will jump to that stage, and the sequencer will
  1804→then loop linearly (honoring the ORDER button’s ‘Forward’ or ‘Reverse’ DIRECTION setting) for
  1805→the number of pulses defined by the Loopy Screen’s LOOP PULSES parameter.
  1806→The LOOPY (∞) button will glow blue for as long as your finger is on a Stage button (or if Loopy
  1807→is latched). The blue LOOPY button indicates you’re currently hearing the track playback via its
  1808→Loopy settings, and not its Track settings).
  1809→NOTE: If LOOP PULSES = ‘Auto’, then the 1-finger loop length is one stage, and the held stage
  1810→simply repeats, playing any and all PULSE COUNTS. The Auto option provides the most utility
  1811→when used with 2-finger Loopy patterns, discussed later.
  1812→4. Lift your finger, then press and hold a different Stage button to shift the loopy region to begin at
  1813→that stage.
  1814→5. Release the held Stage button.
  1815→Loopy returns to playing your original sequence at the point it would be at had Loopy not been
  1816→triggered.
  1817→
  1818→Metropolix Manual
  1819→
  1820→36
  1821→
  1822→ 2-Finger Loopy
  1823→When the track is playing, and you press two Stage buttons, Loopy (on the next clock pulse) begins

  1825→at the second finger’s Stage button. It will still honor the LOOP PULSES count, or (if set to ‘Auto’) it

  1827→Specifically:
  1828→1. Enter and configure Loopy as described in Enter and Configure Loopy Mode.
  1829→2. If the sequencer is currently stopped, press the RUN button (or use one of the remote RUN

  1839→The LOOPY screen’s LOOP PULSES setting further affects the loopy cycle. Specifically:

  1845→those stages.
  1846→For example, assume each stage has a PULSE COUNT = 1, and you hold down the

  1901→There are a few important caveats regarding this mode:
  1902→●
  1903→
